tagline: Upscales images by inventing plausible detail that was never in the original.
verdictSummary: Open-source upscalers are genuinely good and free to run: Real-ESRGAN on a consumer GPU will take a 512-pixel image to 2048 cleanly in seconds. What they will not do is Magnific's actual trick, which is hallucinating detail that never existed — skin pores, fabric weave, brick texture — under a creativity dial. That behaviour comes from a proprietary model trained for it. You can rebuild the workflow around the model; you cannot rebuild the model.
coreLoopDIY: Drop images into a watched folder, run them through a local Real-ESRGAN or SwinIR model at a chosen scale factor, and review the results in a before-and-after slider with the exact settings recorded next to each output.
whatYouLose: the creativity slider that invents new detail rather than sharpening existing detail
usable results on very low-resolution or heavily compressed sources
GPU capacity — a 4x upscale of a large image is minutes on a laptop
the prompt-guided variants that steer what the invented detail looks like
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the output is the product. Nobody buys Magnific for its interface; they buy it because the result looks like a photograph taken at that resolution, and no open weights currently match that on faces and textures.
notes: The honest framing here is a batch runner around open-source upscalers, not a Magnific clone. The gap in output quality is real and named in the prompt rather than glossed over.
prompt:
Build a local batch image upscaler with reproducible settings.

Core loop: point the tool at an input folder. For every image, run a chosen upscaling model and write the result to an output folder alongside a sidecar JSON file recording the model name, scale factor, tile size and any denoise setting used, so any output can be regenerated exactly.

Ship three models behind one interface, downloaded on first use rather than bundled: Real-ESRGAN (general purpose, x2 and x4), Real-ESRGAN anime variant, and a face restoration pass (GFPGAN or CodeFormer) that can be toggled on for portraits. Run them on GPU where one is available and fall back to CPU with a clear warning about how much slower that will be.

Process large images in tiles with overlap, and blend the seams, so a 4x upscale of a 4000-pixel photo does not exhaust VRAM. Show a live queue with per-image progress and let the user cancel without corrupting the output folder.

The review interface is the part that matters: a before-and-after slider at 1:1 pixel scale with synchronised panning, so the user can actually judge whether the upscale helped. Add a compare mode that runs the same source through two different settings and shows them side by side.

State plainly in the README what this does not do: it sharpens and reconstructs detail that is statistically implied by the source, and it does not invent new detail the way a diffusion-based creative upscaler does. Do not add a "creativity" control that silently maps onto a denoise strength — that would misrepresent what the model is doing.

Out of scope: any hosted API, any account system, and training or fine-tuning a model.

faq.q: Can it match Magnific's output on a small, blurry photo?
faq.a: No, and that gap is widest exactly where you most want the tool. Real-ESRGAN reconstructs what is implied by the pixels present; below roughly 256 pixels on the short edge there is not enough signal, and the result reads as smooth rather than detailed. Magnific invents the missing detail, which is a different operation.

A GPU with 8 GB of VRAM handles 4x upscales of typical photos comfortably with tiling. On an Apple Silicon Mac the models run through Metal at usable speed. On a CPU it works but a single 4x upscale can take several minutes, which makes batch runs impractical.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing beyond electricity. The models are open weights, they download once, and everything runs locally. This is the rare case where the DIY version has genuinely zero marginal cost per image, against Magnific's credit-based pricing.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Steering the result. Magnific lets you describe what the invented detail should be and get a different plausible reconstruction each time. Here the model produces one deterministic answer per setting; if you do not like it, your only lever is switching models.
